scenes.title: Shell Scripting Basics
scenes.narration: A shell script bundles a series of commands into a single reusable file, turning manual work into automation you can run with one line.

scenes.title: Anatomy of a Script
bullets: The shebang line at the top tells the system which interpreter to use.
Variables store values you can reuse throughout the script.
Conditionals and loops let the script make decisions and repeat work.
Making it executable with chmod +x lets you run it directly.
scenes.narration: Every script starts with a shebang, the special first line that names the interpreter such as bash. Variables let you capture values once and reuse them, keeping the script readable. Conditionals and loops give the script logic so it can branch and repeat. Finally, marking the file executable turns it into a command you can call by name.

scenes.title: A Simple Backup Script
scenes.code:
#!/bin/bash
SRC="/data/raw"
DEST="/data/backup"

if [ -d "$SRC" ]; then
  cp -r "$SRC" "$DEST"
  echo "Backup complete"
else
  echo "Source not found"
fi
scenes.narration: The shebang declares this file a bash script. Two variables hold the source and destination paths so they are easy to change later. The if statement checks whether the source directory actually exists before copying, and only then performs the backup, printing a friendly message. If the source is missing, the else branch reports the problem instead of failing silently.

scenes.title: From File to Command
scenes.narration: The life cycle is short: write the commands into a file, mark it executable with chmod, then run it by prefixing the name with dot-slash. From that point on, an entire workflow lives behind a single command.

scenes.text: Always quote your variables like "$VAR" — it prevents bugs when paths contain spaces or are empty.
scenes.narration: Quoting variables is the single best habit in shell scripting. It protects your scripts from breaking on spaces or empty values, which are among the most common sources of subtle bugs.
